questions.analysis: However 【线索】前句褒后句贬，构成明显语义反转 前句把每日称重描述为a wonderful way（褒义），后句紧接着说this habit can sometimes hurt more than it __(2)__（贬义、提出风险）。一褒一贬之间需要一个表示转 折的连接词，答案应具备"however/but"的语义。 【选项】A) Besides ✗ 表补充而非转折 B) Therefore ✗ 表因果方向反了 C) Otherwise ✗ 表假设条件下的相反结果 D) However ✓ 标准转折词，承接"好处—风险"反转 However意为"然而"，正好承接前句"a wonderful way"与后句"hurt more than it helps"的褒 【验证】代入后整句为However, when done too often, this habit can sometimes hurt more 第一步 outline 的"总-反"开头完全吻合。

helps 【线索】本句 hurt 与空成反义对照 this habit can sometimes hurt more than it __(2)__中，hurt 表"伤害"，连词 more 帮助"。 【选项】 A) helps ✓ 标准反义对照，hurt vs helps helps"帮助"与 hurt 构成最经典的英语反义对，hurt more than it helps是"弊大于利"的固定表 B) cares ✗ 动作主体不对，且非 hurt 的反义 C) warns ✗ 义近"提醒"但与 hurt 不对照 warns"警告"虽然能与"称重"勉强搭上（提醒体重变化），但与 hurt 不构成反义，hurt more than it warns 语义混乱。 D) reduces ✗ 缺宾语、且语义不对 【验证】代入后this habit can sometimes hurt more than it __(2)__读作"弊大于利"，正好作为第1

solely 【线索】前文用 shift ... from ... to 暗示"由广转窄" weighing myself every day caused me to shift my focus from being generally healthy and physically active, to focusing __(3)__ on the scale中，from 后是"全面健康 【选项】A) initially ✗ 时间维度，错维度 B) solely ✓ "唯一地、仅仅"，正与"generally"反义 solely"仅仅、唯一地"完美对照前文的being generally healthy and physically active——从"广 C) occasionally ✗ 频率"偶尔"，与每日称重事实矛盾 occasionally"偶尔地"是频率副词，但作者明确说weighing myself every day，每日称重不可 D) formally ✗ 方式"正式地"，语义与场景无关 【验证】代入后to focusing __(3)__ on the scale变为"仅仅盯着体重秤"，与前文"generally healthy"形成"广—窄"对照，又顺势引出下一句That was bad for my overall fitness

lowering 【线索】上句揭示"增肌反致体重上升"是动机背景 I had gained weight in the form of muscle mass, but thinking only of __(4)__ the number on the scale, I altered my training program——作者已经因增肌而体重上升， 【选项】A) recording ✗ 只"记"无须改训练，动机不足 recording"记录数字"是被动观察，不会促使作者altered my training program，动机—后果链条 B) lowering ✓ "降低数字"才会驱动作者改训练 C) explaining ✗ "解释数字"语义不通 D) accepting ✗ 若接受数字就不会改训练，与后果相反 accepting"接受"数字意味着作者不在意秤上读数，与紧跟着的"altered my training program"完 【验证】代入后thinking only of __(4)__ the number on the scale, I altered my training

reach 【线索】前句指出新训练与正确训练方式相冲突 That conflicted with how I needed to train to __(5)__ my goals——作者已经设定好健 【选项】A) modify ✗ "修改目标"与练习目的不符 B) set ✗ "设定目标"在训练之前已完成 非"设定"。 C) review ✗ "复审目标"与训练目的无关 D) reach ✓ "达到目标"是 train to 的最自然搭配 reach"达到"目标，是 reach one's goals 的高频搭配，且与全文"为了真正的健身目标该怎么训 【验证】代入后That conflicted with how I needed to train to __(5)__ my goals读作"那与我为达

depiction 【线索】accurate ___ of 努力与进展 = 准确反映/描绘 weighing myself daily did not provide an accurate __(6)__ of the hard work and progress I was making in the gym——作者说每日称重没法"准确反映"努力与进展。空处 【选项】A) definition ✗ "定义"对象是概念非过程 B) depiction ✓ "描绘"努力与进展，正中 accurate 搭配 depiction"描绘、刻画"与 accurate 完美搭配（accurate depiction 是高频搭配），意为"准确反 C) distribution ✗ "分布"对象不对 D) prediction ✗ "预测"指向未来，时态对不上 prediction"预测"指向未来，而原文 the hard work and progress I was making 是已发生事实， 【验证】代入后weighing myself daily did not provide an accurate __(6)__ of the hard work and progress I was making in the gym读作"每日称重无法准确描绘你已付出的努力与进

due to 【线索】前果后因——"改训练"是"体重变化"的原因 It takes about three weeks to a month to notice significant changes in your weight __(7)__ altering your training program——"体重变化"发生在"改变训练计划"之后，是后 【选项】 A) due to ✓ "由于"，标准因果搭配 B) regardless of ✗ "不管"否认因果，与语境相反 C) aside from ✗ "除……之外"语义跑偏 D) along with ✗ "伴随"表共现非因果 【验证】代入后significant changes in your weight __(7)__ altering your training program读 后一句The most __(8)__ changes will be observed in skill level, strength and inches lost做铺垫。

immediate 【线索】前句强调体重变化"慢"，本句应给出"快"的对照 上句It takes about three weeks to a month to notice significant changes in your weight强调体重变化耗时长；本句以 The most ___ changes 开头，紧承其后讲"哪种变化 【选项】A) orderly ✗ "有序的"与时间维度不符 B) rigid ✗ "僵硬的"褒贬不符 C) precise ✗ "精确的"维度错，不与"慢"对照 D) immediate ✓ "即时的"正好与"3 周到 1 个月"形成对照 【验证】代入后The most __(8)__ changes will be observed in skill level, strength and inches

reasons 【线索】第2、3段全是"为什么不该每日称重"的原因 weighing myself every day caused me to shift my focus和weighing myself daily did not provide an accurate __(6)__ of the hard work and progress——前两段都在列举"每 【选项】A) claims ✗ "主张"指尚未证实的说法 B) judgments ✗ "判断"指评价行为 C) reasons ✓ "原因"，承接前两段所有理由 reasons"原因"正好回指前两段列举的所有弊端，构成 for these reasons "基于上述原因"的高频 D) methods ✗ "方法"指代对象与前文不符 【验证】代入后For these __(9)__, I stopped weighing myself every day and switched to a bimonthly weighing schedule __(10)__读作"基于这些原因，我停了日称改为双周"，正好

instead 【线索】stopped ... switched ... 即"换做新做法"对比 I stopped weighing myself every day and switched to a bimonthly weighing schedule __(10)__——前一动作是"停掉旧做法"，后一动作是"换上新做法"。这种"停 A 换 【选项】 A) instead ✓ "取而代之"，正中 stop A switch B 句式 instead"作为替代"完美呼应 stopped ... and switched 的替换关系，句末加 instead 把对比强 B) though ✗ "不过"用作让步，无对照对象 C) again ✗ "又一次"与首次更改不符 D) indeed ✗ "确实"用作强调，与替代关系不符 【验证】代入后I stopped weighing myself every day and switched to a bimonthly weighing

track 【线索】Since weight loss is not my goal 是因 Since weight loss is not my goal, it is less important for me to __(11)__ my weight 【选项】 A) track ✓ "追踪"体重，与"减重不是目标"逻辑契合 B) overlook ✗ "忽视"则不需"less important"修饰 C) conceal ✗ "隐瞒"对象错位 D) report ✗ "汇报"需有接收方 【验证】代入后Since weight loss is not my goal, it is less important for me to __(11)__ my

account for 【线索】并列动词 observe 锚定"观察—理解"语义链 Weighing every other week allows me to observe and __(12)__ any significant weight changes——"observe"是观察，本句紧接讲"That tells me whether I need to __(13)__ my training program"，说明作者不仅观察还要根据观察做决策。空处应填"理解/ 【选项】A) depend on ✗ "依赖"与 observe 不形成递进 depend on"依赖"对象通常是支撑物，不与"观察"并列，也无法解释 weight changes。 B) approve of ✗ "赞成"语义反向 C) hold onto ✗ "抓住不放"对象不对 D) account for ✓ "解释"体重变化，与 observe 形成"看到—解释"递进 account for"解释、说明（原因）"与 observe 并列，构成"观察体重变化→解释体重变化"的标 【验证】代入后allows me to observe and __(12)__ any significant weight changes读作"让我观 察并解释体重的显著变化"，紧接That tells me whether I need to __(13)__ my training

adjust 【线索】上句"解释体重变化"指向"是否要改训练" allows me to observe and __(12)__ any significant weight changes. That tells me whether I need to __(13)__ my training program——根据体重变化决定要不要做的事， 【选项】A) share ✗ "分享"无逻辑必要 B) adjust ✓ "调整"，根据体重反馈改训练计划 adjust"调整"与 training program 是固定搭配（adjust one's training program），并与上 C) confirm ✗ "确认"语义偏弱 D) prepare ✗ "准备"指向新计划 prepare"准备"暗示从头规划，但作者已有 training program，需要的是改而非建。 【验证】代入后That tells me whether I need to __(13)__ my training program读作"那让我知道

results 【线索】"用 weigh-in ___ 获取营养信息"暗示"结果/数据" I use my bimonthly weigh-in __(14)__ to get information about my nutrition as well 【选项】 A) results ✓ "结果"可被解读以获取营养信息 B) features ✗ "特征"对象错 C) rules ✗ "规则"无法用于获取信息 D) tests ✗ "测试"与 weigh-in 重复 【验证】代入后I use my bimonthly weigh-in __(14)__ to get information about my nutrition as well读作"我把双周称重的结果用来获取营养信息"，正与下句If my training intensity remains the same, but I'm constantly __(15)__ and dropping weight构成"看结果—推

hungry 【线索】下句"需要增加每日热量摄入"反推原因为"缺热量" this is a __(16)__ that I need to increase my daily caloric intake——结论是要"增加每日 【选项】A) bored ✗ "无聊"与热量摄入无关 B) anxious ✗ "焦虑"无法由"缺热量"线性解释 C) hungry ✓ "饿"与"掉体重"共因，反推"需增加热量" D) sick ✗ "生病"不能用"加热量"解决 【验证】代入后I'm constantly __(15)__ and dropping weight读作"我一直饿，而且在掉体重"，与

sign 【线索】前文给"饿+掉体重"，本句给"需要加热量" I'm constantly __(15)__ and dropping weight, this is a __(16)__ that I need to increase my daily caloric intake——前是症状证据，后是推论。空处应填"标志/信号"类名词。 【选项】A) principle ✗ "原则"对象错 B) secret ✗ "秘诀"语境不对 C) belief ✗ "信念"对象不对 D) sign ✓ "标志、迹象"，正中"症状指示结论" sign"标志、信号"完美填入 this is a sign that 高频句式，意为"这是一个表明……的信号"，正与 【验证】代入后this is a __(16)__ that I need to increase my daily caloric intake读作"这是一个表

decision 【线索】前文"For these reasons, I stopped"表明是作者自己拿的主意 For these __(9)__, I stopped weighing myself every day——是作者基于前两段原因主动 【选项】A) request ✗ "请求"动作发出者错 B) necessity ✗ "必要性"过于客观、与亲历语境不符 C) decision ✓ "决定"——作者主动作出，正中亲历语境 decision"决定"完美呼应 For these reasons, I stopped 的主动决断，the decision to do sth D) wish ✗ "愿望"未必已落实 【验证】代入后The __(17)__ to stop weighing myself every day has done wonders for my overall health, fitness and well-being读作"停掉日称的决定对我的整体健康、体能和幸福

disappointing 【线索】burden 是负面词，weigh-in 又与"看见数字不如意"挂钩 I no longer carry the burden of a __(18)__ morning weigh-in——burden 是负面词，且 前文I had gained weight in the form of muscle mass 但作者却为"数字"焦虑，可见日称 【选项】 A) disappointing ✓ "令人失望的"，与 burden 同色调 burden 的负面情感同向。 B) surprising ✗ "令人惊讶"偏中性、与 burden 不搭 C) restricting ✗ "限制性的"对象错 D) consuming ✗ "消耗的"语义偏"时间/精力消耗" consuming"耗费的"通常与 time/energy 搭配，单用修饰"早晨称重"不自然，且未必触 发"burden"的情绪意味。 【验证】代入后I no longer carry the burden of a __(18)__ morning weigh-in读作"我不再背负令

because 【线索】主句报喜"取得更大成功"，从句给原因"按目标训练" I've also experienced greater success in achieving my specific fitness goals, __(19)__ I'm training according to those goals, not the numbers on a scale——主句是结果"成 【选项】A) if ✗ "如果"表假设，与已实现的成功矛盾 B) unless ✗ "除非"逻辑反向 C) until ✗ "直到"是时间，非因果 D) because ✓ "因为"，结果 + 原因的标配 【验证】代入后I've also experienced greater success ..., __(19)__ I'm training according to those goals, not the numbers on a scale读作"我也取得了更大的成功，因为我是按目标

obsessing 【线索】对照对象 turn focus to ... 暗示"原本注意力被秤夺走" Rather than __(20)__ over the scale, turn your focus to how you look, feel, how your clothes fit and your overall energy level——被推荐的做法是"把注意力转向感受/外观"， 【选项】 A) obsessing ✓ "过度执着于"——obsess over 是固定搭配，正中对照 obsessing"过度执着于、痴迷于"与 over 构成固定搭配 obsess over，且"痴迷于秤上数字"正 B) dominating ✗ "支配"主宾关系反了 C) puzzling ✗ "困惑"语义不对 D) triumphing ✗ "凯旋、胜过"语义反向 【验证】代入后Rather than __(20)__ over the scale, turn your focus to how you look, feel, how your clothes fit and your overall energy level读作"与其执着于秤上的数字，不如把注意 OVERVIEW · 通读建境 文章是第一人称经验分享：开篇承认Weighing yourself regularly is a wonderful way to stay aware of any significant weight fluctuations，但紧接着用转折点明做得太频反而有害；随 后The __(17)__ to stop weighing myself every day has done wonders for my overall health, fitness and well-being点出全文立场——少称反而更好。 第1段先肯定后转折(this habit can sometimes hurt more than it __(2)__)；第2段亲历——每 日称重让作者偏离训练目标(weighing myself every day caused me to shift my focus)；第3 段补理由——一个月才能看出体重变化(It takes about three weeks to a month to notice significant changes in your weight)；第4段给出新做法——双周称一次(I stopped weighing myself every day and switched to a bimonthly weighing schedule)；第5段延伸用途——用 称重数据判断营养摄入(to get information about my nutrition as well)；第6段总结好处、 第7段升华建议(turn your focus to how you look, feel, how your clothes fit and your overall energy level)。 SENTENCE INSIGHTS · 句子精讲 11 Weighing yourself regularly is a wonderful way to stay aware of any significant weight fluctuations. sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: Unlike so-called basic emotions such as sadness, fear, and anger, guilt emerges a little later, in conjunction with a child's growing grasp of social and moral norms. Children aren't born knowing how to say "I'm sorry"; rather, they learn over time that such statements appease parents and friends – and their own consciences. This is why researchers generally regard so-called moral guilt, in the right amount, to be a good thing. In the popular imagination, of course, guilt still gets a bad rap. It is deeply uncomfortable – it's the emotional equivalent of wearing a jacket weighted with stones. Yet this understanding is outdated. "There has been a kind of revival or a rethinking about what guilt is and what role guilt can serve," says Amrisha Vaish, a psychology researcher at the University of Virginia, adding that this revival is part of a larger recognition that emotions aren't binary – feelings that may be advantageous in one context may be harmful in another. Jealousy and anger, for example, may have evolved to alert us to important inequalities. Too much happiness can be destructive. And guilt, by prompting us to think more deeply about our goodness, can encourage humans to make up for errors and fix relationships. Guilt, in other words, can help hold a cooperative species together. It is a kind of social glue. Viewed in this light, guilt is an opportunity. Work by Tina Malti, a psychology professor at the University of Toronto, suggests that guilt may compensate for an emotional deficiency. In a number of studies, Malti and others have shown that guilt and sympathy may represent different pathways to cooperation and sharing. Some kids who are low in sympathy may make up for that shortfall by experiencing more guilt, which can rein in their nastier impulses. And vice versa: High sympathy can substitute for low guilt. In a 2014 study, for example, Malti looked at 244 children. Using caregiver assessments and the children's self-observations, she rated each child's overall sympathy level and his or her tendency to feel negative emotions after moral transgressions. Then the kids were handed chocolate coins, and given a chance to share them with an anonymous child. For the low-sympathy kids, how much they shared appeared to turn on how inclined they were to feel guilty. The guilt-prone ones shared more, even though they hadn't magically become more sympathetic to the other child's deprivation. "That's good news," Malti says. "We can be prosocial because we caused harm and we feel regret."

Forests give us shade, quiet and one of the harder challenges in the fight against climate change. Even as we humans count on forests to soak up a good share of the carbon dioxide we produce, we are threatening their ability to do so. The climate change we are hastening could one day leave us with forests that emit more carbon than they absorb. Thankfully, there is a way out of this trap – but it involves striking a subtle balance. Helping forests flourish as valuable "carbon sinks" long into the future may require reducing their capacity to absorb carbon now. California is leading the way, as it does on so many climate efforts, in figuring out the details. The state's proposed Forest Carbon Plan aims to double efforts to thin out young trees and clear brush in parts of the forest. This temporarily lowers carbon-carrying capacity. But the remaining trees draw a greater share of the available moisture, so they grow and thrive, restoring the forest's capacity to pull carbon from the air. Healthy trees are also better able to fend off insects. The landscape is rendered less easily burnable. Even in the event of a fire, fewer trees are consumed. The need for such planning is increasingly urgent. Already, since 2010, drought and insects have killed over 100 million trees in California, most of them in 2016 alone, and wildfires have burned hundreds of thousands of acres. California plans to treat 35,000 acres of forest a year by 2020, and 60,000 by 2030 – financed from the proceeds of the state's emissions-permit auctions. That's only a small share of the total acreage that could benefit, about half a million acres in all, so it will be vital to prioritize areas at greatest risk of fire or drought. The strategy also aims to ensure that carbon in woody material removed from the forests is locked away in the form of solid lumber or burned as biofuel in vehicles that would otherwise run on fossil fuels. New research on transportation biofuels is already under way. State governments are well accustomed to managing forests, but traditionally they've focused on wildlife, watersheds and opportunities for recreation. Only recently have they come to see the vital part forests will have to play in storing carbon. California's plan, which is expected to be finalized by the governor next year, should serve as a model.

American farmers have been complaining of labor shortages for several years. The complaints are unlikely to stop without an overhaul of immigration rules for farm workers. Congress has obstructed efforts to create a more straightforward visa for agricultural workers that would let foreign workers stay longer in the U.S. and change jobs within the industry. If this doesn't change, American businesses, communities, and consumers will be the losers. Perhaps half of U.S. farm laborers are undocumented immigrants. As fewer such workers enter the country, the characteristics of the agricultural workforce are changing. Today's farm laborers, while still predominantly born in Mexico, are more likely to be settled rather than migrating and more likely to be married than single. They're also aging. At the start of this century, about one-third of crop workers were over the age of 35. Now more than half are. And picking crops is hard on older bodies. One oft-debated cure for this labor shortage remains as implausible as it's been all along: Native U.S. workers won't be returning to the farm. Mechanization isn't the answer, either – not yet, at least. Production of corn, cotton, rice, soybeans, and wheat has been largely mechanized, but many high-value, labor-intensive crops, such as strawberries, need labor. Even dairy farms, where robots do a small share of milking, have a long way to go before they're automated. As a result, farms have grown increasingly reliant on temporary guest workers using the H-2A visa to fill the gaps in the workforce. Starting around 2012, requests for the visas rose sharply; from 2011 to 2016 the number of visas issued more than doubled. The H-2A visa has no numerical cap, unlike the H-2B visa for nonagricultural work, which is limited to 66,000 a year. Even so, employers complain they aren't given all the workers they need. The process is cumbersome, expensive, and unreliable. One survey found that bureaucratic delays led the average H-2A worker to arrive on the job 22 days late. The shortage is compounded by federal immigration raids, which remove some workers and drive others underground. In a 2012 survey, 71 percent of tree-fruit growers and almost 80 percent of raisin and berry growers said they were short of labor. Some western farmers have responded by moving operations to Mexico. From 1998 to 2000, 14.5 percent of the fruit Americans consumed was imported. Little more than a decade later, the share of imports was 25.8 percent. In effect, the U.S. can import food or it can import the workers who pick it.

Arnold Schwarzenegger, Dia Mirza and Adrian Grenier have a message for you: It's easy to beat plastic. They're part of a bunch of celebrities starring in a new video for World Environment Day – encouraging you, the consumer, to swap out your single-use plastic staples like straws and cutlery to combat the plastics crisis. The key messages that have been put together for World Environment Day do include a call for governments to enact legislation to curb single-use plastics. But the overarching message is directed at individuals. My concern with leaving it up to the individual, however, is our limited sense of what needs to be achieved. On their own, taking our own bags to the grocery store or quitting plastic straws, for example, will accomplish little and require very little of us. They could even be detrimental, satisfying a need to have "done our bit" without ever progressing onto bigger, bolder, more effective actions – a kind of "moral licensing" that allays our concerns and stops us doing more and asking more of those in charge. While the conversation around our environment and our responsibility toward it remains centered on shopping bags and straws, we're ignoring the balance of power that implies that as "consumers" we must shop sustainably, rather than as "citizens" hold our governments and industries to account to push for real systemic change. It's important to acknowledge that the environment isn't everyone's priority – or even most people's. We shouldn't expect it to be. In her latest book, Why Good People Do Bad Environmental Things, Wellesley College professor Elizabeth R. DeSombre argues that the best way to collectively change the behavior of large numbers of people is for the change to be structural. This might mean implementing policy such as a plastic tax that adds a cost to environmentally problematic action, or banning single-use plastics altogether. India has just announced it will "eliminate all single-use plastic in the country by 2022." There are also incentive-based ways of making better environmental choices easier, such as ensuring recycling is at least as easy as trash disposal. DeSombre isn't saying people should stop caring about the environment. It's just that individual actions are too slow, she says, for that to be the only, or even primary, approach to changing widespread behavior. None of this is about writing off the individual. It's just about putting things into perspective. We don't have time to wait. We need progressive policies that shape collective action (and rein in polluting businesses), alongside engaged citizens pushing for change.

Part B Directions: Read the following text and match each of the numbered items in the left column to its corresponding information in the right column. There are two extra choices in the right column. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points) In choosing a new home, Camille McClain's kids have a single demand: a backyard. McClain's little ones aren't the only kids who have an opinion when it comes to housing, and in many cases youngsters' views weigh heavily on parents' real estate decisions, according to a 2018 Harris Poll survey of more than 2,000 U.S. adults. While more families buck an older-generation proclivity to leave kids in the dark about real estate decisions, realty agents and psychologists have mixed views about the financial, personal and long-term effects kids' opinions may have. The idea of involving children in a big decision is a great idea because it can help them feel a sense of control and ownership in what can be an overwhelming process, said Ryan Hooper, clinical psychologist in Chicago. "Children may face serious difficulties in coping with significant moves, especially if it removes them from their current school or support system," he said. Greg Jaroszewski, real estate broker with Gagliardo Realty Associates, said he's not convinced that kids should be involved in selecting a home – but their opinions should be considered in regards to proximity to friends and social activities, if possible. Younger children should feel like they're choosing their home – without actually getting a choice in the matter, said Adam Bailey, real estate attorney based in New York. Asking them questions about what they like about the backyard of a potential home will make them feel like they're being included in the decision-making process, Bailey said. Many of the aspects of homebuying aren't a consideration for children, said Tracey Hampson, a real estate agent based in Santa Clarita, Calif. And placing too much emphasis on their opinions can ruin a fantastic home purchase. "Speaking with your children before you make a real estate decision is wise, but I wouldn't base the purchasing decision solely on their opinions." Hampson said. The other issue is that many children – especially older ones – may base their real estate knowledge on HGTV shows, said Aaron Norris of The Norris Group in Riverside, Calif. "They love Chip and Joanna Gaines just as much as the rest of us," he said. "HGTV has seriously changed how people view real estate. It's not shelter, it's a lifestyle. With that mindset change come some serious money consequences." Kids tend to get stuck in the features and the immediate benefits to them personally, Norris said. Parents need to remind their children that their needs and desires may change over time, said Julie Gurner, a real estate analyst with FitSmallBusiness.com. "Their opinions can change tomorrow," Gurner said. "Harsh as it may be to say, that decision should likely not be made contingent on a child's opinions, but rather made for them with great consideration into what home can meet their needs best–and give them an opportunity to customize it a bit and make it their own." This advice is more relevant now than ever before, even as more parents want to embrace the ideas of their children, despite the current housing crunch. challenges to children.
